title: Myscelus. Croton
titleEn: Myscelus, and the Founding of Croton — Metamorphoses XV.1–59
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: The question is asked who can carry a weight so vast and succeed so great a king, and report marks out Numa. Not content with having learned the rites of the Sabines, he wants to know what the nature of things is, and that question carries him from Cures to a Greek city on the Italian coast, where he asks who founded it. An old man answers him: Hercules, rich with the Iberian cattle he had brought from the Ocean, was made welcome by Croton and promised a city on the spot, and long after appeared in a dream to Myscelus of Argos and ordered him to leave his country — which the law punished with death, until at the count the black voting-pebbles had all turned white. Myscelus sailed to Italy, raised the walls he had been commanded to raise beside Croton's grave and gave the city the dead man's name; the question Numa came with is still standing when these lines end.

sentences.t:
Quaeritur interea quis tantae pondera molis
sustineat tantoque queat succedere regi:
sentences.l: Meanwhile it is asked who may bear the burdens of so great a mass and who could succeed so great a king:
sentences.i: Meanwhile the question is put: who is to carry a weight so vast, who is able to succeed so great a king?
sentences.n: Quaeritur is an impersonal passive, “it is asked”, with nobody named as asking. What follows is an indirect question, which is why sustineat and queat are subjunctive. Moles is a mass or bulk, and pondera molis piles weight on weight — the burden is the state itself. Succedere takes a dative, tanto regi: “to come up under”, hence “to succeed”. The king is not named in these lines.

sentences.t:
destinat imperio clarum praenuntia veri
fama Numam;
sentences.l: Rumour, forerunner of the truth, marks out for the command the renowned Numa;
sentences.i: Rumour, that herald of what proves true, singles out the famous Numa for the throne;
sentences.n: The verb destinat opens line 3, but its subject fama and its object Numam are both held back to the head of line 4, and clarum, which agrees with Numam, is stranded in line 3 on the far side of the line-end. Praenuntia veri, “forerunner of the truth”, is a noun in apposition to fama, and feminine like fama itself. Imperio is dative: Numa is marked out for the rule.

sentences.t:
non ille satis cognosse Sabinae
gentis habet ritus:
sentences.l: He does not hold it enough to have come to know the rites of the Sabine people:
sentences.i: It is not enough for him to have learned the rites of the Sabine people:
sentences.n: Satis habet with an infinitive is “counts it enough to”. Cognosse is the syncopated form of cognovisse, the perfect infinitive; verse uses these short forms constantly, and you will meet intrasse and relevasse for intravisse and relevavisse at line 16. Sabinae goes with gentis across the line-end, and gentis in turn depends on ritus.

sentences.t:
animo maiora capaci
concipit et, quae sit rerum natura, requirit.
sentences.l: With a capacious mind he conceives greater things and asks what the nature of things may be.
sentences.i: With a mind wide enough to hold them he takes in greater matters, and asks what the nature of things is.
sentences.n: Animo capaci is ablative, the mind as the space in which he conceives, with maiora wedged between the noun and its adjective. Maiora is a neuter comparative used as a noun, “greater things”. Quae sit rerum natura is another indirect question, hence the subjunctive sit. Rerum natura, “the nature of things”, is the standing Latin phrase for the physical constitution of the universe, and is the title of Lucretius's poem on it. The question is put here and is not answered anywhere in these fifty-nine lines.

sentences.t:
Huius amor curae, patria Curibusque relictis,
fecit ut Herculei penetraret ad hospitis urbem.
sentences.l: Love of this pursuit, his native land and Cures having been left behind, made him make his way to the city of Hercules' host.
sentences.i: Love of that inquiry — his homeland and Cures once left behind — carried him all the way to the city of the man who had been Hercules' host.
sentences.n: Huius curae is an objective genitive: love directed at that inquiry, not love belonging to it. Patria Curibusque relictis is an ablative absolute, a self-contained “with X left behind” phrase where English wants a clause; it is the first of several in this part, and the later ones will only be pointed at. Fecit ut with the subjunctive penetraret gives the result, “brought it about that he made his way”. Cures is the town he came from. Herculei hospitis urbem, “the city of Hercules' host”, names nobody: the man is Croton, and the tale beginning at line 12 explains how he came to be Hercules' host.

sentences.t:
Graia quis Italicis auctor posuisset in oris
moenia, quaerenti sic e senioribus unus
rettulit indigenis, veteris non inscius aevi:
sentences.l: To him asking what founder had set Greek walls on Italian shores, one of the older natives, not unacquainted with the ancient past, replied thus:
sentences.i: When he asked what founder had raised Greek walls on Italian shores, one of the older natives, no stranger to the old days, answered him so:
sentences.n: Graia opens line 9 and its noun moenia opens line 10, so “Greek walls” is stretched across a whole verse — and the oddity is the point: Greek walls, on Italian shores. Quis auctor is “what man, as founder”, and posuisset is pluperfect subjunctive because the question is being reported. Quaerenti is a dative participle standing in for the man himself, “to him as he asked”. Unus e senioribus … indigenis is broken up too, with e senioribus in line 10 and indigenis in line 11, unus and rettulit standing between them. Veteris non inscius aevi is litotes: “not ignorant of” for “well versed in”.

sentences.t:
“Dives ab Oceano bubus Iove natus Hiberis
litora felici tenuisse Lacinia cursu
fertur
sentences.l: “Jove's son, rich with Iberian cattle from the Ocean, is said to have reached the Lacinian shores on a fortunate voyage
sentences.i: “The son of Jove, rich with the Iberian cattle he had brought from the Ocean, is said to have made the Lacinian shore on a fair passage
sentences.n: Iove natus, “born of Jove”, is Hercules. In these fifty-nine lines he is never called by name: only claviger, “club-bearer” (22), the adjectives Herculei (8) and Herculeo (47), and the patronymic Amphitryoniadae (49). Fertur governs everything the old man now reports: tenuisse here, and intrasse, relevasse and dixisse to come, are perfect infinitives in indirect statement, which is why the English keeps saying “is said to have”. Litora … Lacinia, the shores by the Lacinian headland, and felici … cursu are interwoven, each pair split apart by the other. Bubus … Hiberis is the herd Hercules drove home from the far west — Geryon's, in the myth — and ab Oceano puts it at the western edge of the world.

sentences.t:
et, armento teneras errante per herbas,
ipse domum magni nec inhospita tecta Crotonis
intrasse et requie longum relevasse laborem
sentences.l: and, his herd wandering through the tender grass, to have entered himself the house of great Croton and a roof not unwelcoming, and to have relieved his long toil with rest
sentences.i: and, while the herd strayed over the soft grass, to have gone in himself to the house of great Croton and a roof that turned nobody away, and to have eased his long labour with rest
sentences.n: Armento … errante is another ablative absolute, and it interlocks with teneras … herbas, the four words taken alternately from one pair and the other. Ipse marks the contrast with the herd: the cattle stay outside, the man goes in. Nec inhospita tecta is litotes again, “a roof not unwelcoming”, and it is built on the same root as hospitis at line 8 — the host is being defined by his hospitality before he is named. Intrasse and relevasse are the syncopated perfect infinitives promised at line 4, still governed by fertur. Requie is ablative of means.

sentences.t:
atque ita discedens “aevo” dixisse “nepotum
hic locus urbis erit”;
sentences.l: and so, as he departed, to have said, “In the age of descendants this place will be a city's”;
sentences.i: and so at his going to have said: “In the age of descendants this place will belong to a city”;
sentences.n: The edition marks the interruption of Hercules' words by dixisse with the same curly quotation marks it uses for the old man's own long speech, which opened at line 12 and does not close until line 57 — so “aevo” looks at first glance like the end of the outer speech. It is not: it is the first word of the quoted prophecy, resumed after dixisse at “nepotum”. Aevo nepotum is an ablative of time when, “in the age of descendants”. Urbis is a predicative genitive: the place will be “of a city”, will belong to one.

sentences.t: promissaque vera fuerunt.
sentences.l: and the promises were true.
sentences.i: and the promises proved true.
sentences.n: The chain of infinitives under fertur stops here: fuerunt is a plain indicative, so the old man steps out of reported speech and vouches for the outcome himself, though the quotation runs on to line 57. Promissa is a neuter plural participle used as a noun, “the things promised”. Fuerunt is the full third-plural perfect ending; the poetic short form in -ere turns up at line 39, fecere.

sentences.t:
Nam fuit Argolico generatus Alemone quidam
Myscelos, illius dis acceptissimus aevi.
sentences.l: For there was a certain Myscelus, begotten of Argive Alemon, of that age the most acceptable to the gods.
sentences.i: For there was a man called Myscelus, born of Alemon of Argos, and of all that generation the dearest to the gods.
sentences.n: Generatus takes an ablative of origin, Argolico Alemone, “begotten of Argive Alemon”. The edition keeps the Greek nominative Myscelos rather than latinising it to Myscelus; from Alemon Ovid builds the Greek patronymic Alemonides at 26, with a Greek accusative Alemoniden at 48. Dis is dative with acceptissimus, and illius … aevi a genitive of the whole hanging on the superlative: the most acceptable of that age. Argolico is doing work: the founder of a Greek city in Italy is fetched from Argos.

sentences.t:
Hunc super incumbens pressum gravitate soporis
claviger adloquitur:
sentences.l: Leaning over him — him pressed down by the heaviness of slumber — the club-bearer addresses him:
sentences.i: The club-bearer stooped over him where he lay pressed down by heavy sleep, and spoke:
sentences.n: Hunc super is anastrophe: the preposition super stands after its object, which verse does freely. Pressum agrees with hunc, not with the god — it is Myscelus who is weighed down, by gravitate soporis, “the heaviness of sleep”. Claviger, “club-bearer”, is a title and not a name; the twelve labours at line 39 identify him. Adloquitur is deponent: passive in form, active in sense.

sentences.t:
“Lapidosas Aesaris undas
i, pete diversi! Patrias, age, desere sedes!”
sentences.l: “The stony waters of far-off Aesar — go, seek them! Your ancestral seats, come, abandon!”
sentences.i: “Go, make for the stony waters of far-off Aesar! Leave the home of your fathers — go now!”
sentences.n: Diversi is genitive and belongs with Aesaris, from which three words and the line-end separate it: “of the far-off Aesar”, far off from where Myscelus is, in Argos. Aesar is the river at the site of the city to be, and its adjective returns at line 54, Aesarei. In the Latin the object comes first in each half — lapidosas … undas stands ahead of i, pete, and patrias … sedes closes around age, desere — which is what gives the order its shove, and is more than the English can carry over. Age here is not the verb “drive” but the interjection, “come now”.

sentences.t: et, nisi paruerit multa ac metuenda minatur;
sentences.l: and, unless he shall have obeyed, he threatens many things and things to be feared;
sentences.i: and threatens much, and much to be dreaded, if he will not obey;
sentences.n: Metuenda is a gerundive used as an adjective, “things needing to be feared”. Paruerit is future perfect: inside the god's threat the condition is “if he shall not have obeyed”. A point about the printing: the edition sets a comma after et to open the parenthetic clause and prints no comma to close it — et, nisi paruerit multa ac metuenda minatur; — where the same clause at line 33 is punctuated on both sides, et, nisi paruerit, plura et graviora minari. The sense wants that second comma. The line is given here exactly as the edition prints it, unaltered.

sentences.t: post ea discedunt pariter somnusque deusque.
sentences.l: After that, sleep and the god depart alike.
sentences.i: With that, sleep and the god both withdraw at once.
sentences.n: The doubled -que … -que, somnusque deusque, is a verse mannerism for “both … and”, and setting the two nouns side by side at the line's end makes the sleep and the god leave in a single movement — pariter, “alike, together”. The edition prints post ea as two words where the ordinary adverb is postea.

sentences.t:
Surgit Alemonides tacitaque recentia mente
visa refert, pugnatque diu sententia secum:
sentences.l: Alemon's son rises, and in his silent mind goes back over the fresh-seen things, and long his judgement fights with itself:
sentences.i: Alemon's son gets up, and turns the night's fresh visions over in his silent mind; and for a long while his resolve fights with itself:
sentences.n: Alemonides is the Greek patronymic built on the Alemone of line 19, “Alemon's son”, and it is how the passage names him from here on. Visa is the neuter plural participle of video used as a noun, “things seen”, with recentia, “fresh”. Refert is “carries back”, so “goes back over”. Sententia here is not a verdict but his own settled opinion, and pugnat secum sets that opinion against itself: what the Latin puts in the fight is the sententia, not the man — the same word returns in its courtroom sense at 43 and 47.

sentences.t:
numen abire iubet, prohibent discedere leges,
poenaque mors posita est patriam mutare volenti.
sentences.l: The divine power bids him go, the laws forbid him to depart, and death has been set as the penalty for one wishing to change his native land.
sentences.i: The god commands him to go; the laws forbid him to leave; and death is the penalty laid down for anyone who chooses to change his homeland.
sentences.n: Two clauses set against each other with no connecting word, numen against leges and iubet against prohibent, which is what makes the deadlock audible. Posita est is the ordinary phrase for a penalty laid down by law. Volenti is a dative participle used as a noun, “for one wishing”, and mutare patriam is the offence itself — not treason, not desertion, simply changing the country you belong to. This is the capital charge the rest of the tale turns on.

sentences.t:
Candidus Oceano nitidum caput abdiderat Sol,
et caput extulerat densissima sidereum Nox:
sentences.l: The gleaming-white Sun had hidden his shining head in Ocean, and thickest Night had lifted her starry head:
sentences.i: The white Sun had sunk his gleaming head beneath the Ocean, and Night at her deepest had raised her starry one:
sentences.n: An elaborate way of saying that it had grown dark. The two clauses mirror each other around the repeated caput: abdiderat against extulerat, down against up. In line 31 the two noun-adjective pairs cross each other: after the opening et, caput stands second in the line and its adjective sidereum fifth, while densissima stands fourth and its noun Nox last. Oceano is a bare ablative of place with no preposition, which verse allows. Candidus is worth holding on to: white is about to become the colour that decides the trial — niveis at 41, album at 46, candida at 47.

sentences.t:
visus adesse idem deus est eademque monere
et, nisi paruerit, plura et graviora minari.
sentences.l: The same god was seen to be at hand and to warn the same things, and, unless he shall have obeyed, to threaten more things and heavier.
sentences.i: The same god seemed to stand there and give the same warnings, and to threaten more, and worse, if he did not obey.
sentences.n: Visus est with an infinitive is the personal construction: Latin says “the god was seen to be at hand” where English can also say “it seemed that he was”. Eadem is neuter plural, the object of monere — the same warnings. Line 33 repeats line 24 with everything raised a step: minatur becomes the infinitive minari, and multa ac metuenda becomes plura et graviora, “more things and heavier”. Here the edition does print the comma after paruerit that line 24 lacks.

sentences.t:
Pertimuit patriumque simul transferre parabat
in sedes penetrale novas:
sentences.l: He took fright, and at the same time was preparing to carry his ancestral shrine across into a new dwelling:
sentences.i: He grew thoroughly afraid, and at once set about moving his family's shrine to a new home:
sentences.n: Pertimuit is timeo compounded with per-, frightened right through. The penetrale is the innermost part of a house, where the household gods stood; moving it is not moving furniture but moving the household itself, which is exactly what the law of 28–29 forbids. The adjective patrium sits in line 34 and its noun penetrale in line 35, with simul transferre parabat in sedes standing between them — and in sedes … novas closes around penetrale in its turn.

sentences.t:
fit murmur in urbe,
spretarumque agitur legum reus;
sentences.l: a murmur arises in the city, and he is brought to trial as defendant of the laws flouted;
sentences.i: a murmur runs round the city, and he is put on trial charged with flouting the laws;
sentences.n: Reus takes a genitive of the charge, spretarum legum. Latin puts the accusation into a perfect participle where English wants an abstract noun: “of the laws having been flouted” comes out as “with flouting the laws”. Agitur reus is the technical phrase for standing trial. Fit murmur in urbe is barely a clause — four words, and the whole city has turned.

sentences.t:
utque peracta est
causa prior crimenque patens sine teste probatum,
sentences.l: and when the first pleading had been carried through and the charge, lying open to view, had been proved without a witness,
sentences.i: and when the first hearing had run its course, and the charge, plain as it was, had been proved without a witness called,
sentences.n: Causa prior is the earlier stage of the trial, the pleading, before the verdict. Probatum has its est understood from the peracta est earlier in the same ut-clause; Latin drops a repeated auxiliary freely. The charge needed no witness because the act was open — the murmur of line 35 was the city seeing it. Patens, “lying open”, is what this edition prints; some editions print patet, which makes it a main verb, “and the charge is plain”, without much changing the sense of the sentence.

sentences.t:
squalidus ad superos tollens reus ora manusque
“o cui ius caeli bis sex fecere labores,
fer, precor” inquit, “opem!
sentences.l: the defendant, unkempt, lifting his face and his hands to the gods above — “O you for whom twice six labours made a right to heaven, bring, I beg,” he says, “help!
sentences.i: the defendant, unwashed and unkempt, raised his face and his hands to the gods above and said: “O you whose twice-six labours won you a right to heaven — bring me help, I beg you!
sentences.n: Squalidus is not a comment on the man's character: a defendant went unwashed and in soiled clothes to move the court, and Ovid hands the Roman custom to an Argive Greek without apology. Fecere is fecerunt, the poetic third-plural perfect in -ere that verse uses constantly — the first one in this part, against the full form fuerunt back at line 18. Bis sex, “twice six”, is the twelve labours, and ius caeli is the right to a place among the gods that they earned him. Ora is a plural for a single face, normal in verse. Inquit is dropped into the middle of the plea, and the edition closes and reopens the quotation marks around it.

sentences.t: nam tu mihi criminis auctor.”
sentences.l: for you (are) for me the author of the charge.”
sentences.i: for you are the one who brought this charge upon me.”
sentences.n: Es is left out, as Latin leaves out the verb “to be” constantly; the words are simply “for you, for me, the author of the charge”. Crimen is the accusation rather than the guilt, and the argument is exact: the god commanded the act at 22–23, so the god, not the man, is the auctor, the one who set it going. Mihi is a dative of the person concerned, “in my case”.

sentences.t:
Mos erat antiquus niveis atrisque lapillis,
his damnare reos, illis absolvere culpa;
sentences.l: There was an ancient custom, with snow-white and black pebbles — with these to condemn the accused, with those to absolve from guilt;
sentences.i: There was an old custom of pebbles, snow-white and black: with the black to condemn the accused, with the white to clear them of guilt;
sentences.n: The two infinitives damnare and absolvere spell out what the custom was, an explanatory use English manages with “of condemning … of acquitting”. His and illis are the trap: hic points to the nearer or last-named thing and ille to the further or first-named, so his is the black pebbles and illis the white — and 43–44, where the black stones go into the urn and the sentence is grim, confirm which is which. Culpa is an ablative of separation with absolvere, “to loose from guilt”. Lapillus is a “little stone”, the voting-pebble; the calculus of line 44 is the same object under another name.

sentences.t:
tunc quoque sic lata est sententia tristis, et omnis
calculus inmitem demittitur ater in urnam.
sentences.l: then too the grim sentence was passed in this way, and every pebble goes down black into the pitiless urn.
sentences.i: this time too the grim sentence was passed in that fashion: every pebble drops black into the merciless urn.
sentences.n: Sententiam ferre is the phrase for delivering a verdict, here passive, lata est. Then the tense slips: lata est is perfect and demittitur present, and the present makes the pebbles fall in front of you. Inmitem, “pitiless”, is a transferred epithet — it is the verdict that has no pity, not the urn. Omnis calculus is singular for “every single pebble”, and ater is held back past the verb. Tunc quoque is the plain adverb, “then too”; quoque is sometimes quo-que, “and by which”, but not here. Inmitem is this edition's unassimilated spelling of immitem.

sentences.t:
Quae simul effudit numerandos versa lapillos,
omnibus e nigro color est mutatus in album,
candidaque Herculeo sententia numine facta
solvit Alemoniden.
sentences.l: And as soon as it, turned over, poured out the pebbles to be counted, for all of them the colour was changed from black into white, and the sentence, made white by Hercules' divine power, released Alemon's son.
sentences.i: And the moment the urn was tipped and poured the pebbles out to be counted, the colour of every one of them had changed from black to white, and the verdict, turned white by Hercules' godhead, set Alemon's son free.
sentences.n: Quae is a connecting relative: it looks back to urnam at the end of line 44, and where Latin runs straight on with a relative English starts a new sentence — “and this urn”. Simul on its own here is “as soon as”. Numerandos is a gerundive, “to be counted”, doing the work of an English infinitive of purpose. Omnibus is a dative of the thing concerned, “for all of them”. Numen is a god's power to act, and Herculeo … numine is the ablative of means by which the change is made — and candida then makes the verdict itself white, which is why the passage has been counting colours since line 41.

sentences.t:
Grates agit ille parenti
Amphitryoniadae, ventisque faventibus aequor
navigat Ionium,
sentences.l: He gives thanks to the parent, Amphitryon's son, and, the winds favouring, sails the Ionian water,
sentences.i: He gives thanks to that father of his, Amphitryon's son, and with the winds behind him sails the Ionian sea,
sentences.n: Parens is not a literal father here — Myscelus's father is Alemon, at line 19 — but the god who fathered the whole enterprise and then saved him. Amphitryoniades, “son of Amphitryon”, names Hercules from his mortal stepfather, where line 12 named him from his divine one, Iove natus. Grates agere is the set phrase for giving thanks, and grates rather than gratias is the higher, more solemn word. Ventis faventibus is an ablative absolute. Aequor navigat is an accusative of the space crossed: he sails not on the sea but the sea.

sentences.t:
Sallentinumque Neretum
praeterit et Sybarin Lacedaemoniumque Tarentum
Thurinosque sinus Crimisenque et Iapygis arva
sentences.l: and passes Sallentine Neretum and Sybaris and Lacedaemonian Tarentum and the Thurian gulfs and Crimise and the fields of Iapyx
sentences.i: passing Sallentine Neretum, and Sybaris, and Spartan Tarentum, and the bays of Thurii, and Crimise, and the lands of Iapyx
sentences.n: A coasting catalogue: the single verb praeterit governs the whole string, and the chain of -que and et makes the places go by one after another, which is the effect wanted. Sybarin and Crimisen keep the Greek accusative in -n where a fully latinised form would end in -m. Lacedaemonium Tarentum is “Spartan Tarentum” because the city was a Spartan foundation — the coast is Greek the whole way, which is what Numa asked about at 9–10. The edition prints Thurinosque, the gulf of Thurii; some editions print Sirinosque, naming the Siris instead, a different water on the same shore.

sentences.t:
vixque pererratis, quae spectant litora, terris,
invenit Aesarei fatalia fluminis ora
nec procul hinc tumulum, sub quo sacrata Crotonis
ossa tegebat humus, iussaque ibi moenia terra
condidit et nomen tumulati traxit in urbem.”
sentences.l: and, the lands which look upon those shores having scarcely been wandered over, he found the fated mouth of the river Aesar, and not far from here a mound, beneath which the earth was covering the hallowed bones of Croton, and there on that soil he founded the walls he had been bidden to build, and drew the name of the buried man over onto the city.”
sentences.i: and when he had barely finished ranging the lands that face those shores, he found the destined mouth of the river Aesar, and not far from here a mound, under which the earth lay over the consecrated bones of Croton; and there on that ground he founded the walls he had been ordered to raise, and carried the buried man's name across to the city.”
sentences.n: Vix pererratis … terris is an ablative absolute with its own relative clause, quae spectant litora, wedged inside it. Invenit is the same in the present and the perfect; the condidit and traxit that follow are perfect and pull it that way, so the run of presents at navigat and praeterit settles into past for the founding. Ora is the plural of os and here means the river's mouth — verse uses the plural for the one opening, and it is the same form that meant “face” at line 38, itself a plural for one face. Aesarei picks up the Aesaris of the god's command at line 22: the river he was sent to is the river he finds. Hinc, “from here”, gives the speaker away — the old man is telling this standing on the spot. Iussa moenia are the walls of that command. Tumulati is a participle used as a noun, “the man buried there”, and traxit nomen in urbem, “drew the name across onto the city”, answers the question Numa asked at 9–10. The edition prints litora at 53, the lands that look upon shores; some editions print aequora, that look upon the waters.

sentences.t:
Talia constabat certa primordia fama
esse loci positaeque Italis in finibus urbis.
sentences.l: Such, it was agreed on sure report, were the beginnings of the place and of the city set within Italian bounds.
sentences.i: Such, by settled tradition, were the origins of the place, and of the city planted inside Italian borders.
sentences.n: The old man's speech has closed at line 57 and the poem's own narrator takes the story back. Constabat takes an accusative and infinitive, talia primordia esse — “it was agreed that such were the beginnings”. Certa fama is ablative, “on sure report”, and it answers the fama of lines 3–4, where rumour was called praenuntia veri, the forerunner of truth. Loci and positae … urbis are both genitives depending on primordia, and primordia are “first beginnings”, the very origins. The narrator vouches for the foundation story and stops; the question Numa brought with him at line 6 is left standing.
